BAYH-DOLE ACT — INVENTIONS MADE WITH FEDERAL FUNDING (35 U.S.C. §§ 200-212) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Cascade Biophysics Institute · National Institutes of Health

INVENTIONS MADE WITH FEDERAL FUNDING — WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This information sheet describes the federal statute that allocates patent rights in an invention that was conceived or first actually reduced to practice with federal research money — the Bayh-Dole Act, chapter 18 of the Patent Act, 35 U.S.C. §§ 200-212 — and the Supreme Court decision construing it. It is written around a situation in which Cascade Biophysics Institute performed work funded by National Institutes of Health and a method of stabilizing lyophilized enzyme assays came out of that work.

The question it asks is not the question intellectual-property material usually asks. The usual questions are who owns an invention as between an inventor and an employer, what an assignment has to say to be effective, and what the owner can do about a copier. Those questions are settled by contract and by general patent law. The question here sits on top of them: when the research was paid for in whole or in part by the federal government, a separate federal scheme attaches to the invention and gives a federal agency a bundle of standing rights — a paid-up license, reporting, march-in, a United States manufacture preference — that no private agreement between the inventor and the employer created and that none of them can bargain away on its own.

What follows states the text of 35 U.S.C. §§ 200-212, the standard patent rights clause that the implementing regulation requires funding agreements to contain, and the holding and reasoning of Board of Trustees of the Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc., 563 U.S. 776 (2011). It does not assess whether a method of stabilizing lyophilized enzyme assays is a subject invention, does not say what Cascade Biophysics Institute or Dr. Priya Venkataraman should do, and does not predict how any agency or court would decide anything.

THE DECLARED POLICY OF THE CHAPTER (35 U.S.C. § 200)
Chapter 18 of the Patent Act opens with a statement of congressional policy rather than an operative command. Section 200 lists seven objectives: using the patent system to promote utilization of inventions arising from federally supported research or development; encouraging participation by small business firms; promoting collaboration between commercial concerns and nonprofit organizations, including universities; ensuring that inventions made by nonprofit organizations and small business firms are used in a manner that promotes free competition and enterprise without unduly encumbering future research and discovery; promoting commercialization and public availability of inventions made in the United States by United States industry and labor; ensuring that the Government obtains sufficient rights in federally supported inventions both to meet its own needs and to protect the public against nonuse or unreasonable use; and minimizing the costs of administering these policies. The "without unduly encumbering future research and discovery" language was added in 2000 by Public Law 106-404; the rest of the section is as enacted in 1980. The chapter is popularly known as the Bayh-Dole Act, and also as the University and Small Business Patent Procedures Act of 1980.

WHAT MAKES AN INVENTION A "SUBJECT INVENTION" (35 U.S.C. § 201)
Three defined terms decide whether the chapter reaches a given invention. A "funding agreement" is any contract, grant or cooperative agreement between a federal agency (other than the Tennessee Valley Authority) and any contractor for the performance of experimental, developmental or research work funded in whole or in part by the federal government, and the term also reaches any assignment, substitution of parties, or subcontract of any type entered into for the performance of such work. A "contractor" is any person, small business firm or nonprofit organization that is a party to a funding agreement. A "subject invention" is any invention of the contractor conceived or first actually reduced to practice in the performance of work under a funding agreement. Section 201(g) defines "made," when used of an invention, as the conception or first actual reduction to practice of that invention, so the two acts named in the "subject invention" definition are the two acts that can bring the chapter into play. Section 201(f) defines "practical application," the benchmark used later in the march-in provision, as manufacturing a composition or product, practicing a process or method, or operating a machine or system, under conditions establishing that the invention is being utilized and that its benefits are available to the public on reasonable terms to the extent permitted by law or Government regulations. Section 201(i) defines "nonprofit organization" to include universities and other institutions of higher education and section 501(c)(3) organizations.

ELECTION OF TITLE, AND THE THREE DEADLINES THAT CONDITION IT (35 U.S.C. § 202(A), (C)(1)-(3))
Section 202(a) provides that each nonprofit organization or small business firm may, within a reasonable time after the disclosure required by § 202(c)(1), elect to retain title to any subject invention. The subsection then lists four situations in which a funding agreement may provide otherwise: a contractor not located in or without a place of business in the United States or subject to the control of a foreign government; exceptional circumstances found by the agency; a determination by a foreign-intelligence or counter-intelligence authority; and certain Department of Energy naval nuclear propulsion or weapons facilities. Section 202(b)(1) requires an agency invoking one of those clauses to determine first that the condition exists and, except for the intelligence clause, to file a copy of the determination with the Secretary of Commerce within thirty days of award.

Section 202(c) requires every funding agreement with a small business firm or nonprofit organization to carry provisions effectuating a list of obligations. The first three are timing obligations, and each is paired with the same consequence: the federal government may receive title. The contractor must disclose each subject invention to the agency within a reasonable time after it becomes known to the contractor personnel responsible for administering patent matters. The contractor must make a written election within two years after that disclosure, or such additional time as the agency approves, whether it will retain title. And a contractor electing rights must file a patent application before the expiration of the one-year period referred to in § 102(b), and thereafter file corresponding applications in other countries in which it wishes to retain title within reasonable times.

THE GOVERNMENT’S STANDING LICENSE AND THE GOVERNMENT-SUPPORT STATEMENT (35 U.S.C. § 202(C)(4), (C)(6))
Where the contractor elects rights, § 202(c)(4) requires the funding agreement to give the federal agency a nonexclusive, nontransferrable, irrevocable, paid-up license to practice or have practiced for or on behalf of the United States any subject invention throughout the world. The same paragraph permits the funding agreement to provide additional rights, including the right to assign or have assigned foreign patent rights, where the agency determines they are necessary to meet United States obligations under a treaty, international agreement, arrangement of cooperation, memorandum of understanding or similar arrangement, including a military agreement relating to weapons development and production.

Section 202(c)(6) requires the agreement to obligate the contractor, if a United States patent application is filed by or on its behalf or by any assignee, to include within the specification of that application and any patent issuing from it a statement specifying that the invention was made with Government support and that the Government has certain rights in the invention. The federal license is therefore visible on the face of the issued patent rather than only in the funding file.

CONDITIONS THAT APPLY ONLY TO NONPROFIT CONTRACTORS (35 U.S.C. § 202(C)(7))
Section 202(c)(7) imposes a further set of conditions on funding agreements with nonprofit organizations. Clause (A) requires a prohibition on assigning rights in a subject invention in the United States without agency approval, subject to an exception for assignment to an organization one of whose primary functions is the management of inventions, with that assignee then subject to the same provisions as the contractor. Clause (B) requires that the contractor share royalties with the inventor. WHERE THE INDIVIDUAL INVENTOR APPEARS IN THE STATUTE (35 U.S.C. § 202(D))

MARCH-IN RIGHTS AND THE ROUTE OF REVIEW (35 U.S.C. § 203)
Section 203(a) gives the funding agency the right, following regulations promulgated under the chapter, to require the contractor, an assignee or an exclusive licensee of a subject invention to grant a nonexclusive, partially exclusive or exclusive license in any field of use to a responsible applicant on terms reasonable under the circumstances, and, if the request is refused, to grant such a license itself. The right is conditioned on one of four agency determinations: that action is necessary because effective steps to achieve practical application have not been taken and are not expected to be taken within a reasonable time; that action is necessary to alleviate health or safety needs not reasonably satisfied by the contractor, assignee or licensees; that action is necessary to meet requirements for public use specified by federal regulations that are not reasonably satisfied; or that action is necessary because the United States manufacture agreement required by § 204 has not been obtained or waived, or because a licensee of the exclusive right to use or sell in the United States is in breach of that agreement.

Section 203(b) removes such a determination from chapter 71 of title 41, directs that an administrative appeals procedure be established by regulation under § 206, and allows any contractor, inventor, assignee or exclusive licensee adversely affected to file a petition within sixty days in the United States Court of Federal Claims, which has jurisdiction to determine the appeal on the record and to affirm, reverse, remand or modify. For determinations under paragraphs (1) and (3) of subsection (a), the agency determination is held in abeyance pending exhaustion of those appeals or petitions.

THE UNITED STATES MANUFACTURE PREFERENCE AND ITS WAIVER (35 U.S.C. § 204)
Section 204 restricts exclusive licensing of a subject invention for the United States market. Notwithstanding any other provision of the chapter, a small business firm or nonprofit organization that receives title to a subject invention, and any assignee of such a firm or organization, may not grant any person the exclusive right to use or sell the subject invention in the United States unless that person agrees that products embodying the subject invention, or produced through its use, will be manufactured substantially in the United States.

The section provides for waiver in individual cases. The funding agency under whose agreement the invention was made may waive the requirement on a showing by the firm, organization or assignee either that reasonable but unsuccessful efforts have been made to grant licences on similar terms to potential licensees likely to manufacture substantially in the United States, or that under the circumstances domestic manufacture is not commercially feasible. Failure to obtain or waive the § 204 agreement, and breach of such an agreement by an exclusive licensee, are among the grounds for march-in under § 203(a)(4).

This information sheet describes the federal statute that allocates patent rights in an invention that was conceived or first actually reduced to practice with federal research money — the Bayh-Dole Act, chapter 18 of the Patent Act, 35 U.S.C. §§ 200-212 — and the Supreme Court decision construing it. It is written around a situation in which Cascade Biophysics Institute performed work funded by National Institutes of Health and a method of stabilizing lyophilized enzyme assays came out of that work.

The question it asks is not the question intellectual-property material usually asks. The usual questions are who owns an invention as between an inventor and an employer, what an assignment has to say to be effective, and what the owner can do about a copier. Those questions are settled by contract and by general patent law. The question here sits on top of them: when the research was paid for in whole or in part by the federal government, a separate federal scheme attaches to the invention and gives a federal agency a bundle of standing rights — a paid-up license, reporting, march-in, a United States manufacture preference — that no private agreement between the inventor and the employer created and that none of them can bargain away on its own.

What follows states the text of 35 U.S.C. §§ 200-212, the standard patent rights clause that the implementing regulation requires funding agreements to contain, and the holding and reasoning of Board of Trustees of the Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc., 563 U.S. 776 (2011). It does not assess whether a method of stabilizing lyophilized enzyme assays is a subject invention, does not say what Cascade Biophysics Institute or Dr. Priya Venkataraman should do, and does not predict how any agency or court would decide anything.

Chapter 18 of the Patent Act opens with a statement of congressional policy rather than an operative command. Section 200 lists seven objectives: using the patent system to promote utilization of inventions arising from federally supported research or development; encouraging participation by small business firms; promoting collaboration between commercial concerns and nonprofit organizations, including universities; ensuring that inventions made by nonprofit organizations and small business firms are used in a manner that promotes free competition and enterprise without unduly encumbering future research and discovery; promoting commercialization and public availability of inventions made in the United States by United States industry and labor; ensuring that the Government obtains sufficient rights in federally supported inventions both to meet its own needs and to protect the public against nonuse or unreasonable use; and minimizing the costs of administering these policies. The "without unduly encumbering future research and discovery" language was added in 2000 by Public Law 106-404; the rest of the section is as enacted in 1980. The chapter is popularly known as the Bayh-Dole Act, and also as the University and Small Business Patent Procedures Act of 1980.

In Board of Trustees of the Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc., 563 U.S. 776 (2011), the Supreme Court held that the Bayh-Dole Act does not automatically vest title to a federally funded invention in the federal contractor, and does not authorize a contractor to take title unilaterally. Stanford and the United States as amicus curiae had argued that the Act reorders the normal priority of rights when an invention is conceived or first reduced to practice with federal support, moving inventors from the front of the line to the back.

The Court rejected that reading on four grounds. First, where Congress has divested inventors it has said so unambiguously, as in the atomic energy, space and Department of Energy statutes the Court cited, and such language is absent from the Bayh-Dole Act. Second, the definition of "subject invention" is limited to an invention "of the contractor," a phrase the Court read as denoting ownership and which would be surplusage on Stanford’s reading. Third, § 202(a) speaks of a right to "elect to retain title," and one cannot retain what one does not already have. Fourth, § 202(d) speaks of the agency granting "requests for retention of rights by the inventor." The Court added that § 210(a)’s precedence provision, which applies only to subject inventions, does not displace an inventor’s antecedent title, and that the Act contains no procedural protection for inventors or for third parties, which makes sense only if the Act operates after a contractor has already acquired the inventor’s interest. The Court observed that contractors generally institute policies to obtain assignments from their employees and that, with an effective assignment, the statute works much as Stanford said it should.
